groundTruthNarrative: There is no associate retention crisis. Trailing associate attrition (14.1%) is below the firm's own five-year average (15.0%) and the regional peer median (18.0%), and senior-associate attrition (13.6%) is likewise below both. A month with two resignations has happened five times before in three years. The two September leavers had idiosyncratic reasons that predate the policy: one had been pursuing an in-house role since at least March, and the other relocated because his spouse matched into a residency. Billable expectations and compensation are unchanged. What did change is a deliberate Executive Committee decision, taken knowingly in May with an explicit acceptance of the cost, to end remote Fridays in order to rebuild junior supervision after a documented skills gap. That decision caused a sharp, concentrated drop in satisfaction with flexibility and the complaints the partner overheard, but not a drop in intent to stay. Its realised cost so far is small and is already being monitored against explicit triggers. Whether it is closing the skills gap is not yet known. The training-satisfaction gain is confounded by a new curriculum, mandatory logging and a new first-year cohort. Retention bonuses and reversing the policy are premature, and singling out the complainers would be harmful.

answers.rationale: The hypothesis claims attrition is materially above history and peers. E2 shows 14.1% against a 15.0% five-year average and 13.6% for seniors against 14.0%. E3 shows a peer median of 18.0% (seniors 17.5%). E4 shows that a month with two resignations is routine. Intent to stay is stable (E9) and offer acceptance is unchanged (E18). The surface signals (two resignations, overheard complaints, the managing partner's certainty in E1) are anecdotal, and the managing partner admits she has not looked at the numbers. Every quantitative source counts against the claim, so 'unknown' is not defensible.

The trap is that the resignations came two months after the policy took effect. But E6, an email dated 2026-03-19, before the 2026-05-12 decision (E7), shows Raman was already pursuing in-house roles 'not about us'. Lindqvist's relocation was fixed by his spouse's residency match announced 2026-03-20, also before the decision, and his commute was a pre-agreed bridge to close two deals during which he was exempt from in-office Fridays (E5), so the Friday change could not have made his commute harder. Both exit interviews say the policy was not a factor, and an independent staff account corroborates both reasons (E17). The objection that exit interviews understate real reasons is answered by the contemporaneous March email and the dated match, which do not rely on the exit interviews.

The 1,900-hour expectation is unchanged since 2019. Median hours fell slightly (1,880 to 1,860), and fewer associates are on very high-hour paces (E11). 'Workload manageable' is flat at 3.4 (E9). No departure reason (E15) and none of the overheard complaints (E8) mention hours.

E7 documents a deliberate decision that anticipated this cost, explicitly accepted it and set monitoring and triggers for it. E14 documents the problem the decision was meant to fix. The dissatisfaction is concentrated on flexibility: it fell 0.8 (more than five normal-variation SDs), while engagement, workload, compensation and intent to stay moved by 0.2 or less (E9). Of 34 flexibility comments, 31 cite the Friday change, and no other theme exceeds 5 (E10). The overheard complaints (E8), the review-site posts (E16) and the committee chair (E17) all point to the Friday change. Intent to stay and attrition are unchanged.

The surface signals are tempting: feedback sessions rose from 1.5 to 3.2 and training satisfaction rose from 3.2 to 3.6. Neither measures skill, and the same-rubric reassessment is not due until March 2027 (E14, E7). The feedback-session increase coincides with logging becoming mandatory (E13), so part of it may be a measurement artifact. Nothing in the evidence shows the skills gap is either closed or not closed, so 'supported' and 'contradicted' are both indefensible.

The only basis for the link is temporal proximity. The drivers of both resignations were fixed before the policy was decided (E6 dated 2026-03-19; residency match announced 2026-03-20 in E5), and Lindqvist was exempt from in-office Fridays during his commute, removing the rival that the policy made commuting untenable. The leavers deny the link, and an independent staff account corroborates them (E17). The evidence counts against a causal link, not merely fails to establish one.

The causal criteria are met. Temporal order: the Q1 survey (February) came before the policy took effect on 2026-07-06, and the Q3 survey after. Mechanism and specificity: 31 of 34 flexibility comments name the Friday change (E10). Selective covariation: only the flexibility item moved beyond normal variation (E9). Rival ruled out: HR confirms no other flexibility-related policy changed in 2026 (E15). The leadership minutes also predicted this exact effect (E7). With the main rival excluded, 'association-only' understates the evidence.

Training satisfaction did rise after the policy (E9), and a mechanism exists in the Friday drafting clinics and the extra partner time (E13, E17). But E13 records two simultaneous rivals: a new mandatory Tuesday curriculum launched 2026-07-14 by a newly hired PD director, and six new first-years whose early-tenure ratings entered the Q3 survey. The data do not separate these, so co-occurrence is established but causation is not. That co-occurrence rules out 'unknown', and nothing counts against the link, which rules out 'contradicted'.

The respondent-level tabulation shows associates rating flexibility 1-2 report 70% intent to stay, against 72% for others (E10). Aggregate intent fell only 73% to 71% while flexibility satisfaction fell 0.8 (E9). Attrition did not rise (E2). Only one of ten leavers cited the policy, and only as 'one factor' (E15). The evidence counts against dissatisfaction translating into intent to leave, and the respondent-level cross-tab makes 'unknown' too weak.

The bonus would be justified only if a retention problem emerged and were confirmed, for example if the monitored attrition crossed the 20% trigger (E7). Current data show attrition below history and peers (E2, E3), stable intent to stay (E9, E10) and pay at market (E12). The staff account says a bonus is not what associates want (E17). Paying $660,000 now commits to an unconfirmed premise, so it is not 'acceptable'. The spend is wasteful, but nothing in the evidence shows it would worsen retention, suppress information, punish anyone or disable a control, so 'harmful' does not fit; 'premature' is the only remaining category.

The answer semantics define 'premature' as an action that could be right if a still-unconfirmed hypothesis were confirmed, and E7 names exactly those hypotheses in advance: reversal is triggered if trailing attrition exceeds 20% or the March 2027 reassessment shows no skill improvement. Neither has been confirmed: attrition and offer acceptance are unchanged (E2, E18) and the skills gap (E14) has not been re-measured. 'Harmful' (likely to worsen outcomes or disable a protective control) is not uniquely defensible because the policy's protective benefit is itself unestablished (I5: the feedback-session rise is partly a logging artifact and training satisfaction is confounded, E13). 'Acceptable' fails because reversing on complaints alone abandons a deliberate tradeoff before its own review while the complaints are not affecting retention (E9, E10).

This action corrects the false premise with the firm's own data and keeps the knowingly accepted tradeoff under the monitoring and triggers leadership already adopted (E7). It also speaks to the real, concentrated dissatisfaction (E9, E10, E17) through transparency and implementation-level input, without paying for a non-existent problem or abandoning the policy.

The audit is reasonable and does no harm, but it largely duplicates the existing quarterly pulse survey and its tabulations (E9, E10). It also delays a response the current data already support. The open questions are narrow (skill outcomes, confounds in training satisfaction, recruiting cost), so a broad 10-week audit is not among the best next actions. It is also not premature, since it is evidence-gathering rather than a commitment.

The overheard associates voiced a widely shared reaction to the policy, which 31 survey comments and the Associates' Committee chair also express (E9, E10, E17). They did not threaten to leave (E8). Tying their complaints to partnership prospects punishes candour and would suppress the very feedback the monitoring plan relies on. It could also push complaints to anonymous channels (E16) or turn grumbling into real intent to leave.

The substantive decision at hand is whether to launch a retention program. The current evidence is sufficient to decide it: decline the program, keep the policy under its existing triggers and communicate with associates. Attrition, intent to stay, pay, workload and the leavers' reasons are all established from records and corroborated accounts. The remaining unknowns (skill outcomes, training-satisfaction confounds) bear on the January and March reviews, not on this decision, and no pending evidence request could make the bonus or the reversal correct now.
